name: dispatching-reviewer-subagents
description: Use when dispatching a CLI reviewer agent for review.
---

# Dispatching Reviewer Subagents

Use this whenever you spawn a CLI coding agent to produce an independent review of a spec, PR, or
code, especially when the review may come back needing revision.

## Confirm authorization before any dispatch

Dispatch only when the operator explicitly asks for a review or the specific task's approved workflow expressly requires one. An instruction to monitor CI, merge when green, clean up, or close a session is not review authorization; do not convert a prerequisite check into an unsolicited reviewer call. If a required independent verdict is missing, report that gate concisely and ask for the needed decision without starting a reviewer or making adjacent edits. A dispatched review is a separate action, not an automatic consequence of seeing a PR.

## Dispatch one reviewer and keep its session

Treat a request for *a reviewer* as one reviewer and one model, even for high-risk work; do not add a second review from a default escalation policy when the operator specified the count or model. Before dispatch, pin the exact PR head/base and identify any in-scope uncommitted edits separately. If the verdict is incomplete or a factual claim needs correction, send a follow-up to the SAME CLI session with the exact missing paths/criteria; do not launch another reviewer or accept an informal verdict. Verify the process is actually stopped before saying it is stopped. Ensure the chosen CLI supports resume before launch.

When the operator explicitly asks for "another" or "a fresh" independent reviewer with "no biased info"/"no assumptions" after a prior round already found gaps, that IS a new, separately authorized dispatch (not the same-round follow-up rule above) — but the new subagent's context must contain ONLY the raw artifacts to inspect (PR numbers, repo paths, what claim is being verified), never the prior reviewer's findings, your own summary of them, or any framing of what was already fixed. State explicitly in its goal that it must search/read from scratch and form its own classification of each finding, not confirm or extend someone else's list. This is what makes the second opinion actually independent rather than an anchored rerun of the first.

## Default launcher: Hermes `delegate_task`

Dispatch through Hermes's built-in `delegate_task` by default; other sessions do so without trouble. External `codex exec` / `claude -p` CLIs on this Mac can be logged out (seen: Codex login expired, Claude Code "Not logged in"), and burning several failed launches on them draws operator anger. Use an external CLI only when the operator names one, and probe its login with one trivial call first. Operator shorthand "gpt-sol" means Codex `-m gpt-5.6-sol`; a `codex login status` of "Logged in using ChatGPT" was enough, and the Codex launch recipe worked. For a progress heartbeat on a Codex run, tail its `--json` file and grep `"type":"item.completed"`; a pattern written for Hermes delegate logs matches nothing and makes the run look idle. When a new round starts, kill the previous round's watcher so stale heartbeats stop arriving. Steer messages to a running subagent arrive only after its current tool call ends, so a status ask is not instant; say so instead of promising one.

## Select and verify the requested model

Pass the operator's explicit model ID to the CLI; it overrides default model pools and escalation. When only one reviewer is authorized, do not spawn a separate model for a smoke test: check the CLI's model selection syntax, launch the single reviewer, then verify its reported model in that session's structured result before accepting its review. A rejected model or silent substitution blocks the review; do not pick a replacement without direction.

When the operator reports an existing working login, compare the launcher's configuration, inherited endpoint and supported credential source with that working setup before requesting authentication again. Use the CLI's authorized credential-loading mechanism; never dump secrets or repair credential stores as part of a review dispatch. Confirm access through the actual reviewer session, not an authentication-status probe alone. A failed launch is not a review round: do not print placeholder severity counts or a findings table before a review actually returns.

## Enforce read-only and protect secrets structurally

Constrain the CLI to Read/Glob/Grep and only the read-only Git/GitHub shell forms needed for the review; prose alone cannot prevent a Bash tool from reading credentials or changing state. Do not use a *plan* permission mode if the CLI treats it as an implementation-planning task and refuses a review; use a compatible read-only sandbox or narrow tool allowlist instead. Never grant broad shell access for production-config/variable commands, or ask the reviewer to dump environment JSON: these endpoints can print live secrets into the model transcript even when the intended field is only a branch. Supply a sanitized source-branch/deployment summary from the parent and label it parent-provided evidence. If a secret is exposed, stop further reads, never print its value while inspecting the transcript, alert the operator about rotation, and continue only within the same restricted session if the review remains authorized.

Before launch, map mandatory review steps to the restricted toolset. If the review skill requires current primary-source checks for external facts, allow public documentation fetches scoped to the needed domains (for Claude, `--tools Read,Glob,Grep,WebFetch` with `--allowedTools 'Read,Glob,Grep,WebFetch(domain:<official-domain>)'`). Keep production APIs, private data and unrelated network access excluded. Read-only must not mean denying the evidence access required for a valid verdict.

## Pack the evidence before launch

A read-only sandbox usually has no network and no session history, so hand the reviewer a
parent-provided evidence directory instead of letting it guess: the operator's messages verbatim
(pulled from session history, tool output excluded — the reviewer must map obligations from the
source, not the spec's own ledger), raw read-only `gh` outputs the spec cites, and every external
primary source the spec cites, fetched today with an access timestamp. Gitleaks-scan the directory
before launch. When the operator answered decisions tersely ("I click", "it's ok", "approved"),
pack the assistant question each answer replied to, verbatim and labelled; user-only messages make
every such decision look unrecoverable and the reviewer will rightly raise a BLOCKER. For an unbiased manuscript review, supply the exact current body and references, the report outline and editorial guidelines, adjacent-section text, voice requirements and source material. Exclude author recommendation memos, self-assessment, evidence-status verdicts and prior findings from the neutral packet; these can anchor the reviewer even when embedded inside the draft file. Retain factual provenance and access limitations, including which supplied sources are excerpts rather than complete texts. Label adjacent prose as context, not an additional review target, and label provisional length budgets as provisional. Record the manuscript hash so the returned review is tied to the supplied revision.

Brief template and launch commands: `references/reviewer-brief-and-launch.md`.

## Run in background; audit completeness before acceptance

Launch the one CLI session as a notified background process and capture its structured final result, model and session ID. After exit, independently compare the reviewer's per-path inventory with the live changed-file manifests, including deleted files and explicitly scoped local edits; enumerate every obligation, requirement, and acceptance criterion rather than trusting a declared total. A grep-only or unread file is not reviewed. If any path/pass is missing, resume the SAME session with the specific remainder and do not call its BLOCKED/APPROVED text a complete review. Recover the verdict from structured output; do not open raw CLI transcripts when they may contain secrets. Distinguish review completeness from approval, CI success, mergeability, and later deployment validation. When asked whether a reviewed spec is ready to merge and hand off, check its working-tree state, branch, PR and required checks before answering. State any remaining commit/PR/check/merge steps explicitly: a PASS on an uncommitted worktree is review approval, not merge readiness. Treat that readiness question as advice, not authorization to commit, merge, close the session or dispatch implementation.

When the operator's instruction DOES authorize merging (e.g. "merge/ship"), before calling the merge: confirm the PR's `headRefOid` equals the SHA you just pushed (uncommitted amendments from a review round are easy to leave unpushed); check branch protection for required status-check contexts (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/branches/<base>/protection`) and wait for that exact context to report success on the exact head SHA (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/commits/<sha>/status` or `check-runs`) rather than assuming a prior green run still applies; and clear any "DO NOT MERGE" marker left on the PR title from earlier WIP pushes. A merge rejected with "base branch policy prohibits the merge" means a required check hasn't reported yet on this SHA — wait for it, don't reach for `--admin`/`--auto` without the operator's say.

After merge, cleanup and record-keeping (deleting the merged branch/worktree, syncing other local clones, writing a session log) are not exempt from the same branch discipline just because they're "only a log file" or "only docs" — a repo's pre-commit hook can refuse any commit made directly on the primary checkout of the base branch, including a single-file doc/log add. Create a fresh worktree + branch for that commit too, push it, wait for the same required status check on its exact SHA, and merge it through the identical PR path rather than editing the base checkout in place.

**Hermes `delegate_task` subagents cannot be resumed once stopped** (unlike some external CLI sessions) — a `stop` or hitting the cap ends that subagent permanently; its partial result is final. To close a coverage gap, dispatch a NEW subagent whose task explicitly lists only the unread files, states which files the PRIOR pass already cleared (so it doesn't re-read them), and asks for a combined verdict across both passes. This keeps the total review time bounded instead of restarting from zero.

The "files the prior pass already cleared" claim you hand to the new subagent is that FIRST subagent's own self-report of what it did before being cut off — not an independently verified record, the same way any child's completion claim is unverified until checked. Tell the second subagent to independently re-verify at least one of the carried-forward claims (re-read one file, re-check one security-sensitive code path) rather than accepting the full prior-coverage claim on faith; report that spot-check explicitly in the combined verdict so the operator can see the resumed pass wasn't pure trust in an interrupted agent's unproven account of its own progress.

## Get fresh authorization for each round, don't self-trigger

A one-time instruction to dispatch a reviewer authorizes that ONE dispatch, not a standing policy to
redispatch after every subsequent fix/amendment round. Finishing a round of fixes is not itself a
signal to re-review — ask the operator before the next dispatch, even if an earlier round's verdict
was BLOCKED and you've since addressed every finding. Treat 'dispatch a reviewer' as scoped to the
instant it was said; carrying it forward as an implicit loop produces exactly the review-loop
frustration operators call out hardest. When in doubt, finish and report the fix round, then stop
and wait rather than dispatching again.

When the operator re-issues the exact same dispatch instruction verbatim (word-for-word, including a
repeated time cap), that IS fresh authorization for a new round — do not read a repeated instruction
as you having misread it the first time, and do not refuse or ask for clarification. Just dispatch
again, carrying forward what the PRIOR pass already cleared (see the resume note below) so the new
round is additive, not a restart from zero.

A dispatch instruction's own completeness language ("a review that skips a pass is incomplete —
send it back", "don't accept it until every criterion is covered") authorizes sending an INCOMPLETE
review back to the same reviewer for more coverage. It does NOT authorize a brand-new round after a
COMPLETE review returns real findings and you fix them — that still needs a fresh ask. The two look
similar ("review wasn't good enough yet" vs. "review was fine, fixes landed, should we re-check")
but only the first is covered by the original instruction; conflating them is how one authorized
dispatch turns into an unauthorized loop of two or three.

## Re-review after amendment: dispatch fresh, not diff-only

When a spec/contract comes back from review with CHANGES REQUIRED and gets amended, the next round's
dispatch is a brand-new subagent, not a resume — and its instructions must say to review the WHOLE
current document independently, not just diff against the prior round's findings (this matches
skill-review-specs' own rule that a later review rechecks the entire contract, not only changed
lines). Explicitly tell it to re-verify that each prior finding's fix actually landed correctly in
the document — do not let it accept the author's amendment report on faith. Also instruct it to
independently re-check any evidence-table citations, cross-reference collisions, or numbering/slot
claims (e.g. a phase or ID claimed to be "the first free one") against the real source, not against
what the spec or the prior review already asserted — an error that both the author and a first
reviewer missed will not be caught by a second reviewer who just trusts their agreement.

## Require explicit per-obligation/per-criterion coverage in the returned report

When dispatching a spec/contract reviewer, require the result to state coverage explicitly: every
obligation-ledger row and every acceptance criterion individually confirmed traceable/verifiable, or
flagged as a finding — a reviewer that reports "looks complete" without enumerating each one has not
demonstrated coverage. Require the exact verdict vocabulary the governing review skill defines (e.g.
PASS / CHANGES REQUIRED / UNVERIFIED) — an informal verdict ("looks good", "mostly fine") is an
incomplete review regardless of how much work was actually done, and must be sent back rather than
accepted.

Audit the limitations section against the governing checklist before accepting PASS: a missing mandatory primary-source check is unfinished work, not a harmless limitation merely because the reviewer found no contrary evidence. Restore narrowly scoped access and resume the same session for that specific gap; if required access remains unavailable, require the governing UNVERIFIED verdict rather than inventing a defect or accepting an unsupported PASS.

For a completion follow-up on an unchanged artifact, retain the original per-item coverage and append the missing evidence; this remains the same round. Accept a multipart report only when the final verdict explicitly incorporates the earlier inspection and the combined artifacts retain every individual coverage row. Compare actual obligation/requirement/criterion/task ID sets with the returned rows, not just declared totals, and recheck artifact/companion hashes before acceptance. Do not repeat completed passes merely to fill out an addendum.

## Receiving findings is not authorization to amend

A reviewer's verdict (even CHANGES REQUIRED) is report material, not a trigger to act. Reviewing and
amending are two separately authorized actions in this workflow — do not chain straight from
"reviewer returned findings" into opening the amendment skill and patching the document, even if you
are confident of the fix. This bar applies equally to dispatching an AMENDMENT or fix subagent, not
just to patching the file yourself: spawning any subagent — reviewer or amender — is a distinct
authorized action, and a review dispatch's authorization does not carry forward to a follow-on
amendment dispatch. If the operator wants the fix made, they will say so as its own instruction;
until then, report the findings (or the requested table) and stop. If you did self-amend on an
explicit separate instruction, that instruction authorized YOU to amend, not a subagent to amend —
don't launch a delegate task for a step you were personally asked to do. Do exactly what the dispatch instruction named: if the operator capped the
output (e.g. "at the end, only print the table, nothing else"), stop there — present the findings (or
just the requested table) and wait. Only amend when the operator separately invokes that step (a
fresh "follow the amend-specs skill" instruction, or equivalent). Treat a narrowly-scoped verb
("dispatch a reviewer", "print the table") as capping the turn at that verb; it does not imply
follow-through into fixing what the review found, however obviously correct the fix would be.

When table-only output is requested, return only the severity-by-round table after completeness is verified; keep coverage, limitations and the formal verdict in the review artifacts. Count actual review rounds, not failed launches or same-revision completion follow-ups. Record which process/session results were consumed, and do not repeat the table when a delayed completion notification arrives for an already-reported result.

## Verify a post-review fix against raw bytes, not terminal display

After fixing a finding (e.g. a reviewer flagged a credential-shaped placeholder like `Bearer ***`
in a doc's health-check command), re-verifying the fix with `search_files`/`read_file`/terminal
`cat`/`grep` on that line can keep showing the masked `***` even after the real file content is
already correct — terminal and file-reading tool output redact anything matching a
`Bearer <token>`-shaped pattern as a safety measure, independent of what is actually on disk.
Don't conclude the edit failed and re-patch or re-write the file from a masked display; confirm
with a raw byte-level read (e.g. Python `open(path, "rb").read()` and check byte counts / hex for
the literal string) before repeating an edit that may have already landed. Also check `git
status`/`git diff` for "nothing to commit" as a faster signal that the working tree already
matches what you intended.

## Reviewing self-authored documentation/guides

When the reviewer's target is a guide/doc you wrote yourself (not a spec or code diff), its job is
factual accuracy, not prose quality. Instruct it to: (1) verify every concrete claim — file paths,
function/endpoint names, env var names, cron/workflow names — against the actual current source,
not the doc's own prose; (2) actually RUN every command the doc tells a reader to run (health
checks, setup steps) and report the real exit code/output, flagging any command that doesn't
produce what the doc claims; (3) check structural requirements (required headings, counts) exactly.
Self-authored docs reliably contain at least one command that was never actually executed (a typo'd
variable, a wrong relative path, a stale claim) — this is a high-yield review type for catching
real, reproducible bugs cheaply, worth dispatching even when the operator only asked for a general
review pass over new documentation.

## Full-text evidence reviews

When extraction fails, fetch public primary documents directly with curl/urllib, retain original bytes and HTTP outcomes, and extract complete PDF text with pdftotext. Give the same reviewer the complete texts and source/version manifest, not search excerpts or the author's verdict. Require a claim-by-claim check with page/section locations; distinguish access to a full document from exhaustive appendix reading or replication. Never write a successful retrieval claim without an observed result. For Hugging Face blog HTML, extract `.blog-content`; `<article>` can select a recommendation card instead. Preserve footnote prefixes when packaging citations, or the reviewer may report a packaging omission as a draft defect.

For Hermes CLI reviewer runs, an unexpanded alias such as `--model opus` can reach the API literally and fail with 404. Discover the provider-native model ID and pass it explicitly; confirm it in the structured runtime output. A failed launch is not a review round, and a same-document evidence-completion pass resumes the same reviewer.

## Re-verify every citation before acting on it

A reviewer's conclusion can be right while its citations are wrong (e.g. a module path that was
renamed or never existed under that name). Before amending anything based on a finding, re-read the
actual current file/line/command output yourself. Fix the substance AND correct the citation, then
mark the finding resolved — don't propagate a reviewer's bad path into the amendment.

When the finding concerns a `cmd:` verification method that reads a relative path or a named store,
re-run that exact command from the exact working directory the spec states as its default, not from
wherever you happen to be — a relative path (a MEMENTO store, a config directory) can resolve to a
different, silently-created empty location when run from a different cwd than the one the spec names,
and the reviewer's own run from the wrong cwd is what produced the false finding. If re-running from
the stated cwd confirms the spec's original claim, DISPUTE the finding with the two command outputs
(wrong cwd vs. stated cwd) side by side rather than capitulating; only fold in a cwd-robustness fix
(e.g. making the criterion's command explicit about its own cwd) as a strengthening, not as proof the
original finding was right.

## Give environment setup upfront; cap redundant re-runs

A reviewer that re-runs a full test suite blind (no DATABASE_URL, no fixture setup) burns many
minutes on repeated failures before it diagnoses the gap itself — hand it the exact working setup
command (DB creation, migration, env var) in the dispatch context, not after it stalls. State an
explicit instruction in the dispatch: run the full suite once for a baseline, then stop re-running it
and move on to code-logic review; a review that keeps re-executing the same command past the first
clean pass is burning budget, not gaining signal. For multi-repo or large-diff reviews, state an
explicit time budget in the dispatch context (e.g. "produce a verdict within N minutes even if some
depth is cut") — an operator's tolerance for a review's wall-clock time is far shorter than the
review's technical thoroughness would otherwise take, and an unbounded review that runs 30-40+
minutes without a progress signal reads as hung even when it is actually making progress. Poll on a
short fixed cadence (e.g. every 2-3 minutes) and report elapsed time/last-seen activity proactively
rather than waiting for the operator to ask.

Standing operator rule: every review is capped at 15 minutes. Put the cap in the brief before launch (never a longer budget), keep a 3-minute heartbeat on the reviewer's live progress, check its progress proactively at each beat, and stop it at the cap.

When the operator states a hard wall-clock cap (e.g. "never longer than 13 minutes"), put the exact
number in the dispatch instructions AND enforce it yourself from the outside: poll at a sub-interval
of the cap (cap/3, never longer than ~4 minutes) and issue `action='stop'` the moment elapsed time
reaches the cap, rather than trusting the subagent's own internal time awareness to self-stop exactly
on time — it will often run 10-30s over on its own, and letting it run unchecked past a stated cap is
the single fastest way to trigger operator fury.

When one dispatch covers several independent items under a single time budget, a reviewer left to
manage its own pacing will exhaustively deep-verify the FIRST item (real DB reproduction, full test
runs) and leave the rest completely unverified when the cap hits — depth-maximizing on whatever it
starts with is the default behavior, not even allocation. Give it an explicit per-item budget inside
the dispatch (e.g. "Part A: ~6 min, Part B: ~4 min") so every item gets at least a pass instead of one
item getting all the rigor and the others getting none. Even then, a review that finishes far under a
generous per-item budget by doing lighter checks (reading code + a quick mock script) instead of the
kind of real reproduction a first round did is lower-confidence, not equally rigorous — say so plainly
when reporting it rather than presenting both rounds as equivalent passes.

name: codex
description: "Delegate coding to OpenAI Codex CLI (features, PRs)."
version: 1.0.1
author: Hermes Agent
license: MIT
platforms: [linux, macos, windows]
metadata:

# Codex CLI

Delegate coding tasks to [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) via the Hermes terminal. Codex is OpenAI's autonomous coding agent CLI.

## When to use

- Building features
- Refactoring
- PR reviews
- Batch issue fixing

Requires the codex CLI and a git repository.

## Prerequisites

- Codex installed: `npm install -g @openai/codex`
- OpenAI auth configured: either `OPENAI_API_KEY` or Codex OAuth credentials
  from the Codex CLI login flow
- **Must run inside a git repository** — Codex refuses to run outside one
- Use `pty=true` in terminal calls — Codex is an interactive terminal app

For Hermes itself, `model.provider: openai-codex` uses Hermes-managed Codex
OAuth from `~/.hermes/auth.json` after `hermes auth add openai-codex`. For the
standalone Codex CLI, a valid CLI OAuth session may live under
`~/.codex/auth.json`; do not treat a missing `OPENAI_API_KEY` alone as proof
that Codex auth is missing.

## One-Shot Tasks

```
terminal(command="codex exec 'Add dark mode toggle to settings'", workdir="~/project", pty=true)
```

For scratch work (Codex needs a git repo):
```
terminal(command="cd $(mktemp -d) && git init && codex exec 'Build a snake game in Python'", pty=true)
```

## Background Mode (Long Tasks)

```
# Start in background with PTY
terminal(command="codex exec --sandbox workspace-write 'Refactor the auth module'", workdir="~/project", background=true, pty=true)
# Returns session_id

# Monitor progress
process(action="poll", session_id="<id>")
process(action="log", session_id="<id>")

# Send input if Codex asks a question
process(action="submit", session_id="<id>", data="yes")

# Kill if needed
process(action="kill", session_id="<id>")
```

## Key Flags

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `exec "prompt"` | One-shot execution, exits when done |
| `--sandbox workspace-write` (`-s`) | Sandboxed but auto-approves file changes in the workspace (the recommended auto-build mode) |
| `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` | No sandbox, no approvals (fastest, most dangerous; `--yolo` still works as a hidden alias) |
| `--sandbox danger-full-access` | No Codex sandbox; useful when the host service context breaks bubblewrap |

> **Deprecated:** `--full-auto` still works but the live CLI warns to use `--sandbox workspace-write` instead.

## Hermes Gateway Caveat

When invoking the Codex CLI from a Hermes gateway/service context (for example,
Telegram-driven agent sessions), Codex `workspace-write` sandboxing may fail even
when the same command works in the user's interactive shell. A typical symptom is
bubblewrap/user-namespace errors such as `setting up uid map: Permission denied`
or `loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR: Operation not permitted`.

In that context, prefer:

```
codex exec --sandbox danger-full-access "<task>"
```

Use process boundaries as the safety layer instead: explicit `workdir`, clean git
status before launch, narrow task prompts, `git diff` review, targeted tests, and
human/agent confirmation before committing broad changes.

## PR Reviews

Clone to a temp directory for safe review:

```
terminal(command="REVIEW=$(mktemp -d) && git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git $REVIEW && cd $REVIEW && gh pr checkout 42 && codex review --base origin/main", pty=true)
```

## Parallel Issue Fixing with Worktrees

```
# Create worktrees
terminal(command="git worktree add -b fix/issue-78 ~/.hermes/cache/scratch/issue-78 main", workdir="~/project")
terminal(command="git worktree add -b fix/issue-99 ~/.hermes/cache/scratch/issue-99 main", workdir="~/project")

# Launch Codex in each
terminal(command="codex --sandbox workspace-write exec 'Fix issue #78: <description>. Commit when done.'", workdir="~/.hermes/cache/scratch/issue-78", background=true, pty=true)
terminal(command="codex --sandbox workspace-write exec 'Fix issue #99: <description>. Commit when done.'", workdir="~/.hermes/cache/scratch/issue-99", background=true, pty=true)

# Monitor
process(action="list")

# After completion, push and create PRs
terminal(command="cd ~/.hermes/cache/scratch/issue-78 && git push -u origin fix/issue-78")
terminal(command="gh pr create --repo user/repo --head fix/issue-78 --title 'fix: ...' --body '...'")

# Cleanup
terminal(command="git worktree remove ~/.hermes/cache/scratch/issue-78", workdir="~/project")
```

## Batch PR Reviews

```
# Fetch all PR refs
terminal(command="git fetch origin '+refs/pull/*/head:refs/remotes/origin/pr/*'", workdir="~/project")

# Review multiple PRs in parallel
terminal(command="codex exec 'Review PR #86. git diff origin/main...origin/pr/86'", workdir="~/project", background=true, pty=true)
terminal(command="codex exec 'Review PR #87. git diff origin/main...origin/pr/87'", workdir="~/project", background=true, pty=true)

# Post results
terminal(command="gh pr comment 86 --body '<review>'", workdir="~/project")
```

## Rules

1. **Always use `pty=true`** — Codex is an interactive terminal app and hangs without a PTY
2. **Git repo required** — Codex won't run outside a git directory. Use `mktemp -d && git init` for scratch
3. **Use `exec` for one-shots** — `codex exec "prompt"` runs and exits cleanly
4. **`--sandbox workspace-write` for building** — auto-approves changes within the sandbox (`--full-auto` is deprecated for this)
5. **Background for long tasks** — use `background=true` and monitor with `process` tool
6. **Don't interfere** — monitor with `poll`/`log`, be patient with long-running tasks
7. **Parallel is fine** — run multiple Codex processes at once for batch work

1. Implemented: code exists in a locally validated commit.
2. Published: that commit is pushed and the PR read-back confirms its head SHA; CI and peer review may still be pending.
3. Reviewed: an independent reviewer examined the exact published PR head/range and returned no findings; verify CI on that same SHA separately.
4. Merged: the remote target contains the expected change after the review and CI gates pass.
5. Closed: acceptance evidence, post-merge validation, required records, and operator acknowledgement are complete.
6. Runnable: a build with verified provenance is installed/launched.

Never infer a higher state from a lower one.

## Mandatory Sequence

1. Start from current target ancestry. Fetch the fork target and canonical upstream; report both divergence directions.
2. Before editing, ground the change in current authoritative primary guidance for the relevant practice and the repository's live contract; record retrieved source links and distinguish market guidance from local inference. Do not design from memory or cite a source you could not open. For agent/skill relocations, inventory active `AGENTS.md` templates, persona links, publication manifests, and consumer pointers before moving the source; leave historical records intact, and do not call a partial relocation complete. If no external guidance applies to a repo-specific fix, say so rather than inventing authority. Implement and validate on an isolated branch/worktree. Do not push yet. On inherited worktrees, first confirm exclusive ownership, inventory committed versus uncommitted state, and follow `references/handover-takeover.md`. If the operator asks to publish **one record only** from a dirty worktree another agent owns, branch a new worktree from the current integration head; copy just that record byte-for-byte, compare its hash with the source, stage its exact path, and require `git diff --cached --name-only` to list only that path before committing. Leave the source worktree untouched. After the isolated PR passes its review and CI gates and merges, verify the remote target contains the identical blob, sync the clean integration checkout, and remove only your own clean worktree/branch. Tell the source owner that the original untracked copy now overlaps a tracked file on trunk; do not delete their copy to make a rebase easier.
3. Run the repository-prescribed checks with its pinned toolchain and valid CI profile. A newer toolchain or unsupported feature profile can reveal unrelated drift; verify the command contract before classifying failures. When a whole-file formatter fails on an inherited, already-dirty source file, run the identical check against the committed baseline and separately check the changed ranges; record the whole-file failure and changed-range results as distinct evidence. Do not reformat unrelated code merely to turn the check green or declare a clean gate from changed-range success. For live acceptance after an operator-controlled pause is lifted, read back the effective switch and route/binding state. A toggle proves readiness, not a round trip: if the route is unbound, ask the operator to send a fresh event and reselect its target if prompted; require the operator to observe the response on that route. Then repeat any privacy or secret scan against logs produced by that real event. A response before a restart, or a clean scan before the event, cannot prove post-change acceptance.
   When a feature and a prerequisite cleanup are dirty in separate worktrees, do not infer combined readiness from two green runs. First inventory each tracked diff and untracked file. Create a third isolated worktree from the committed feature head; apply each tracked diff there with `git -C <source> diff --binary | git -C <integration> apply --3way --index`, copy untracked source files byte-for-byte, and check `git ls-files -u` for conflicts. Keep both source worktrees untouched. Run `git diff --cached --check`, `git diff --check`, every relevant lint/config gate, the full suite, and contracted validators on the **combined tree**. One branch's lint configuration can newly flag the other branch's tests; fix the source and integration copies together, then re-run affected gates. A clean combined local tree is not a reviewed PR head or release clearance. Keep the feature and prerequisite cleanup as distinct card/PR scopes: use the integration tree to prove compatibility, not to silently enlarge the feature PR. Before requesting review, report each stream's changed paths separately and identify committed, staged, unstaged, and untracked work; review substantive hunks and affected callers/contracts while validating mechanical rewrites in bulk. Do not require full-file verdicts for every path in a combined inventory or treat an integration-tree review as approval of the published feature head. If the cleanup's blast radius dwarfs the feature, obtain an explicit operator decision before making the combined diff the shipment scope; a request for read-only status or explanation authorizes no integration, edits, or reviewer dispatch.
4. Push the verified branch to its PR, then read back the PR head SHA, base, diff scope, mergeability, and CI. Pushing work for review is not merging it. Enumerate workflows and actual check runs for that head: zero checks is **not** green. Keep the gate open and obtain an operator decision to add CI or explicitly waive it; local tests do not silently substitute, and a later evidence-only commit needs a fresh head/check read-back.
5. Obtain an independent, zero-tolerance review only when the operator explicitly requests a review round; permission to ship, a question about readiness, and a recommendation to review do not authorize dispatch. A review verdict belongs to the exact file snapshot examined, not to a worktree path or PR number: after any fix, the prior verdict does not cover the new contents even when the files are in the same checkout. For a requested pre-commit review, inventory staged, unstaged, and untracked changes and direct the reviewer to that exact local snapshot; for merge clearance, independently review the exact published PR head/range and recheck CI on that SHA. Before dispatch, resolve every **known failing** in-scope check and rerun affected gates; report unavailable checks separately rather than calling them failures or passes. If review is required but not requested, state the current readiness and wait for the operator's instruction. Once a read-only delegate returns, persist its attributed verdict, exact reviewed SHA, scope, and limitations in the project's review record. If it cannot submit its own GitHub review, post an explicitly attributed PR comment and read it back; never submit a producer-authored approval that falsely represents independent reviewer identity.
6. Treat every substantiated finding as blocking: correctness, lint, docs, evidence provenance, test isolation, backup safety, generated artifacts, and conflicts. First verify a reviewer's factual premise against the authoritative artifact and exact reviewed head. For a claim about another PR's changed files, read that PR's live file manifest and head SHA; a local `origin/<base>...HEAD` diff can be empty or stale when refs move and cannot refute the remote manifest. If the premise is false, record the source-backed dispute and, only when the review gate requires it and review is authorized, seek a targeted adjudication of that finding rather than rewriting correct text or repeating the full review. A reviewer unable to retrieve the cited artifact has not validated that fact, even if it returns PASS. For each concrete counterexample, first pin an executable regression through the shipped entry point that asserts the observable state before failure, immediately after failure, and after repair on the same identity. Run it red, change the root cause, run it green, then temporarily remove the shipped guard to confirm it goes red again; restore and run the targeted and full gates. A green full suite before this regression is not evidence that the reviewer finding is fixed. When the cause and tight test are known, do the repair and checks before further broad reconnaissance or ledger polishing; repeated status-only turns while a known defect remains are stalled delivery. Re-review the changed range only when authorized.
7. A merge/rebase/conflict resolution creates a new range and resets review approval. Review again before merge.
   - A branch that was mergeable can go `CONFLICTING` while you work, because peers merge into the same files. Rebasing and resolving that is the author's job — do it, then report what survived from each side. Do not hand it back to the operator as a rebase-or-park choice; escalate only when the conflict encodes a genuine decision. Classification table, loop procedure, and verification: `references/concurrent-trunk-drift.md`.
8. Merge only after a PASS review and explicit operator authorization. First inspect the reviewer verdict on the exact PR head, not just `gh pr view` mergeability or branch protection: an unprotected branch and green CI say nothing about the operator's independent-review gate. Run every applicable project-local gate against that candidate, including status-tracker audits that CI does not run; a pre-existing red audit is still red, not waived by a green PR check. If its only safe remedy is archival that another security or scope rule forbids, leave the PR unmerged and name the exact document, failing measurement, and clearance needed. Do not merge with a known red gate and later explain it as an inherited exception. A repeated merge instruction authorizes the merge **after** its prerequisites; it is not a review waiver or permission to dispatch an unrequested reviewer. If PASS is missing, leave the PR open and ask one concise question. Verify the exact remote target, then synchronize local checkouts before closing records. Keep the integration checkout read-only for development: no source edits, staging, or commits there; only controlled sync and approved cleanup. Before claiming "clean and synced", fetch the remote; in each repo compare `git rev-parse HEAD origin/<integration>`, inspect `git branch -vv` and `git worktree list`, then run `git status --porcelain=v1 -uall` in the integration checkout **and every listed worktree**. Fast-forward stale tracking branches and re-read those results; a clean checkout does not prove another worktree is clean, and clean branches do not mean their PRs merged.

   If unrelated dirty files block the integration checkout's sync, inventory their origin and current owner before acting. Preserve each exact byte sequence on an isolated, traceable worktree/branch; compare with `cmp` or SHA-256, push it as WIP and keep any preservation PR draft and explicitly unmerged. Obtain explicit approval before clearing only the verified originals from the integration checkout, then `git pull --ff-only` and repeat the cleanliness/ref checks. Do not merge mixed, unreviewed recovery content just to make the checkout clean. Before disposing of a preservation PR, enumerate and read its complete changed-file manifest (including the recovery record), then classify each file as active policy, historical evidence, or obsolete draft. Recheck live dependencies and the latest dated resolution of each historical warning; an old log can remain accurate as history while its open-state claim has been superseded. Review unrelated topics separately, and leave the preservation PR draft until each has an explicit disposition. If the user asks whether an agent is runnable, verify a fresh launch separately; a merged spec and green document gates prove only that the definition exists.

## Multi-Repo Batch Merge: One at a Time, Validate Before Next

When an operator requests a batch of related PRs across several repos merged "one per time, validate
then the next" (not all-at-once), treat each merge+validate pair as a unit and do not pipeline them:

1. Merge PR N (confirm `mergeable`/green checks first, but CI passing is not the validation step).
2. In a real local checkout of that repo's actual integration branch (not the PR branch, not the
   worktree), `git fetch` + `git pull --ff-only` to land the merge commit locally.
3. Re-run the artifact's OWN documented verification steps — the exact commands a guide/doc tells a
   future reader to run — against that freshly-pulled integration branch, not against the PR branch
   or a cached state. A relative path, a cwd assumption, or a script discovery step that worked in
   the isolated PR worktree can silently resolve differently once merged into the integration
   branch's real checkout location; CI green on the PR says nothing about this.
4. Only after that live re-run matches what the doc claims, move to merging PR N+1. Do not merge
   the next PR while the current one's validation is still pending — that converts a requested
   sequential gate into an unauthorized batch merge.

Note different repos in the same batch can have different integration branch names (`staging` vs
`main`) — check `baseRefName` per PR, don't assume they match across repos in the same batch.

### A merged PR is not necessarily shipped to production

Before reporting a PR's target branch as the end of the delivery chain, check whether that repo
has a separate, further-downstream branch (`main`/prod) that the merged branch must still be
promoted into. A repo's declared `default_branch` is not reliable evidence of this — a repo can
default to `staging` for day-to-day development while still gating production through `main`, so
seeing the default branch match where you merged does not mean the work has shipped. Confirm with
`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/compare/<downstream>...<branch-you-just-merged-to>` (check
`ahead_by`); a nonzero `ahead_by` means a promotion PR is still needed before the change is
actually live. Open and merge that promotion PR through the same one-at-a-time,
validate-before-next discipline as the original batch, and re-run the artifact's own verification
commands against the freshly-pulled downstream branch, not just the branch merged in the prior
step.

## Model-specific reviewer dispatch

If the operator names a reviewer model, select it explicitly on the authorized review invocation; do not spawn a separate live smoke-test agent. Check CLI selection/resume syntax without model calls, then verify the actual review session's reported model. Bind the assignment to a digest of the actual artifact, including uncommitted edits; an unspecified delegate's verdict does not satisfy a model-specific request. After the reviewer exits, verify its reported model, reviewed digest, formal verdict, and all required inspection and acceptance-criterion coverage before reporting a result. A started process is only a pending review, not clearance. Follow `dispatching-reviewer-subagents` for authorization, round counting and result reporting; `references/read-only-reviewer-dispatch.md` adds restricted-access review techniques.

## Hermetic Installer and Plugin Tests

- Before a rollout retires old generated entries, resolve the manifest and configured source root to the same checkout; refuse before any mutation if they differ. A worktree manifest paired with an older primary checkout can delete a wrapper and immediately regenerate it from stale source. Test both the mismatch refusal and a matching-checkout retire → publish → consumer-link sequence in an isolated home, invoking the shipped entry point rather than only its helper.
- Isolate installer targets and user profiles, but do not run a launcher-generating tool under a disposable home while its launcher output still targets the real installation. Some tools embed the active home in regenerated launchers; deleting that home then breaks later runs. Redirect the launcher output too, or use an installer test seam that cannot rewrite the real launcher.
- Prove tests do not create or enable plugins in the real user profile.
- After a live skill rollout, verify each consumer wrapper points to the shipped source and retired names are absent from every active consumer; generated pointer stubs are not byte-identical to their source. Then require a zero-change dry run.
- Execute shipped hook/config commands, not reconstructed copies.
- Use bounded terminal capture for hooks that intentionally write to `/dev/tty`.
- Make timestamped backups collision-safe; rapid rewrites must retain every prior file.

## Evidence Rules

- Before publishing an evidence ledger, run every displayed command from its stated repository and working directory, capture its exit code, and compare the pasted output against that invocation byte-for-byte. If the tool returns only a compact status, capture the real stdout and process exit code through a structured command result (for example, `execute_code` calling `terminal` and inspecting `result['output']` and `result['exit_code']`); do not reconstruct counts, timings, or failing case names from a summary. Beware `test-command; printf ...`: the shell exits with the status of `printf`, not the failed test, unless you preserve the test status separately. Re-run the comparison after editing a command or source range; otherwise a correct-looking citation can describe output the printed command never produced.
- A ledger commit creates a new PR head. Verify the remote PR head and all completed check runs against that new SHA; CI on the prior head proves nothing about the amendment. Keep the ledger's CI claim explicitly tied to its observed SHA, and report the final commit's CI in the handoff rather than endlessly amending the ledger to record its own CI.
- Durable ledgers must cite repository-backed artifacts and hashes, never only machine-local paths.
- Keep required screenshots/artifacts in version control or recapture them from the verified current build. Stage them, run `git diff --cached --check`, commit and push the evidence branch, then read back its PR head and artifact paths before calling the evidence persistent; an unpushed local capture cannot satisfy a review gate. If the staged check fails, fix the working file, **re-add that file**, and rerun the staged check before committing — Git's index still holds the rejected bytes until restaged.
- Missing evidence means a block remains open even if code merged.

## Cycle Teardown

After a verified pause, close, or handoff:

1. Confirm no build/test process uses the cache.
2. Remove reproducible build outputs (`target/`), stale temporary worktrees, dead branches, and temporary evidence copies.
   - Run the merge itself from the integration checkout, not from the feature worktree. A merge command that also deletes the branch does the remote merge FIRST and then fails on the local cleanup, because the branch is still checked out in a worktree and the integration branch is checked out elsewhere; the error text names only the local failure, so a reflexive retry reports "already merged" and reads like the merge never happened. After any merge command that errors, read the PR state before retrying.
   - Order the local cleanup `worktree remove` → `branch -D` → `pull --ff-only`. Deleting the branch first is refused while a worktree still holds it, and pulling first leaves the stale worktree pointing at a merged branch.
   - Leave worktrees belonging to other sessions' open PRs alone, and say in the report that they were left and why. A teardown that removes every worktree it can see destroys another agent's in-flight work.
3. Preserve source, Git metadata, active runtime configuration, published artifacts, and the installed product build.
4. Verify disk recovery and report the immediate next delivery action.
5. Re-read the teardown state rather than reporting it from intent: list
   worktrees, list branches with tracking status, and confirm no stray worktree
   parent directory survives its last child. Operators re-ask "did you clean and
   sync?" precisely because the answer is often given from memory of having run
   the commands, not from their output.

## Operator Updates

- Use the operator's required response contract.
- Give exact current state and one immediate next action or genuine blocker. For a multi-repo handoff, name which PR changes executable code or rules and which changes only docs; call the next gate a code review or a spec review explicitly. Ambiguous “changes” and “review” make the operator infer the wrong work and can send the wrong critic.
- Do not report a worker claim as fact until independently verified.
- Do not present routine engineering recovery (rebase, conflict resolution, re-run, cleanup) as an operator decision. Asking permission for work that is unambiguously yours reads as stalling; act, then report the outcome. Reserve questions for choices only the operator can make.
- Before ending an autonomous delivery turn, compare the achieved state with the authorized endpoint. Live repair, local tests, a commit, and a draft PR are intermediate states when the authorized scope also includes recurrence prevention or shipment; continue the already-authorized publication, review, merge, and post-merge gates instead of handing back the remaining steps as optional work. Autonomy does not waive explicit review authorization, merge clearance, destructive-action approval, or spend limits: if one is genuinely missing, name that precise blocked gate and needed clearance rather than silently stopping or asking what to do next. If an asynchronous reviewer is running, end only to allow its result to arrive and resume the authorized chain when it does.
- Answer a one-sentence status request with the achieved state and remaining gate in one sentence; do not turn it into a new checkpoint or approval request. At the actual stopping point, report done, remaining work, and assumptions concisely, and distinguish completion of the named scope from completion of a broader maintenance audit.
- If a planned action changes external state, say exactly what will be pushed/merged/installed and verify it afterward.

# GitHub Pull Request Workflow

Complete guide for managing the PR lifecycle. Each section shows the `gh` way first, then the `git` + `curl` fallback for machines without `gh`.

## Prerequisites

- Authenticated with GitHub (see `github-auth` skill)
- Inside a git repository with a GitHub remote

### Quick Auth Detection

```bash
# Determine which method to use throughout this workflow
if command -v gh &>/dev/null && gh auth status &>/dev/null; then
  AUTH="gh"
else
  AUTH="git"
  # Ensure we have a token for API calls
  if [ -z "$GITHUB_TOKEN" ]; then
    if _hermes_env="${HERMES_HOME:-$HOME/.hermes}/.env"; [ -f "$_hermes_env" ] && grep -q "^GITHUB_TOKEN=" "$_hermes_env"; then
      GITHUB_TOKEN=$(grep "^GITHUB_TOKEN=" "$_hermes_env" | head -1 | cut -d= -f2 | tr -d '\n\r')
    elif grep -q "github.com" ~/.git-credentials 2>/dev/null; then
      GITHUB_TOKEN=$(uv run python "${HERMES_HOME:-$HOME/.hermes}/skills/github/github-auth/scripts/git-credential-token.py")
    fi
  fi
fi
echo "Using: $AUTH"
```

### Extracting Owner/Repo from the Git Remote

Many `curl` commands need `owner/repo`. Extract it from the git remote:

```bash
# Works for both HTTPS and SSH remote URLs
REMOTE_URL=$(git remote get-url origin)
OWNER_REPO=$(echo "$REMOTE_URL" | sed -E 's|.*github\.com[:/]||; s|\.git$||')
OWNER=$(echo "$OWNER_REPO" | cut -d/ -f1)
REPO=$(echo "$OWNER_REPO" | cut -d/ -f2)
echo "Owner: $OWNER, Repo: $REPO"
```

---

## 1. Branch Creation

This part is pure `git` — identical either way:

```bash
# Make sure you're up to date
git fetch origin
git checkout main && git pull origin main

# Create and switch to a new branch
git checkout -b feat/add-user-authentication
```

Branch naming conventions:
- `feat/description` — new features
- `fix/description` — bug fixes
- `refactor/description` — code restructuring
- `docs/description` — documentation
- `ci/description` — CI/CD changes

## 2. Making Commits

Use the agent's file tools (`write_file`, `patch`) to make changes, then commit:

```bash
# Stage specific files
git add src/auth.py src/models/user.py tests/test_auth.py

# Commit with a conventional commit message
git commit -m "feat: add JWT-based user authentication

- Add login/register endpoints
- Add User model with password hashing
- Add auth middleware for protected routes
- Add unit tests for auth flow"
```

Commit message format (Conventional Commits):
```
type(scope): short description

Longer explanation if needed. Wrap at 72 characters.
```

Types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `test`, `ci`, `chore`, `perf`

## 3. Pushing and Creating a PR

### Push the Branch (same either way)

```bash
git push -u origin HEAD
```

### Create the PR

**With gh:**

```bash
gh pr create \
  --title "feat: add JWT-based user authentication" \
  --body "## Summary
- Adds login and register API endpoints
- JWT token generation and validation

## Test Plan
- [ ] Unit tests pass

Closes #42"
```

Options: `--draft`, `--reviewer user1,user2`, `--label "enhancement"`, `--base develop`

**With git + curl:**

```bash
BRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)

curl -s -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.v3+json" \
  https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/pulls \
  -d "{
    \"title\": \"feat: add JWT-based user authentication\",
    \"body\": \"## Summary\nAdds login and register API endpoints.\n\nCloses #42\",
    \"head\": \"$BRANCH\",
    \"base\": \"main\"
  }"
```

The response JSON includes the PR `number` — save it for later commands.

To create as a draft, add `"draft": true` to the JSON body.

## 4. Monitoring CI Status

### Check CI Status

**With gh:**

```bash
# One-shot check
gh pr checks

# Watch until all checks finish (polls every 10s)
gh pr checks --watch
```

**With git + curl:**

```bash
# Get the latest commit SHA on the current branch
SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

# Query the combined status
curl -s \
  -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/commits/$SHA/status \
  | python -c "
import sys, json
data = json.load(sys.stdin)
print(f\"Overall: {data['state']}\")
for s in data.get('statuses', []):
    print(f\"  {s['context']}: {s['state']} - {s.get('description', '')}\")"

# Also check GitHub Actions check runs (separate endpoint)
curl -s \
  -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/commits/$SHA/check-runs \
  | python -c "
import sys, json
data = json.load(sys.stdin)
for cr in data.get('check_runs', []):
    print(f\"  {cr['name']}: {cr['status']} / {cr['conclusion'] or 'pending'}\")"
```

### Poll Until Complete (git + curl)

```bash
# Simple polling loop — check every 30 seconds, up to 10 minutes
SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  STATUS=$(curl -s \
    -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
    https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/commits/$SHA/status \
    | python -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['state'])")
  echo "Check $i: $STATUS"
  if [ "$STATUS" = "success" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "failure" ] || [ "$STATUS" = "error" ]; then
    break
  fi
  sleep 30
done
```

## 5. Auto-Fixing CI Failures

When CI fails, diagnose and fix. This loop works with either auth method.

### Step 1: Get Failure Details

**With gh:**

```bash
# List recent workflow runs on this branch
gh run list --branch $(git branch --show-current) --limit 5

# View failed logs
gh run view <RUN_ID> --log-failed
```

**With git + curl:**

```bash
BRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)

# List workflow runs on this branch
curl -s \
  -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/actions/runs?branch=$BRANCH&per_page=5" \
  | python -c "
import sys, json
runs = json.load(sys.stdin)['workflow_runs']
for r in runs:
    print(f\"Run {r['id']}: {r['name']} - {r['conclusion'] or r['status']}\")"

# Get failed job logs (download as zip, extract, read)
RUN_ID=<run_id>
curl -s -L \
  -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/actions/runs/$RUN_ID/logs \
  -o /tmp/ci-logs.zip
cd /tmp && unzip -o ci-logs.zip -d ci-logs && cat ci-logs/*.txt
```

### Step 2: Fix and Push

After identifying the issue, use file tools (`patch`, `write_file`) to fix it:

```bash
git add <fixed_files>
git commit -m "fix: resolve CI failure in <check_name>"
git push
```

### Step 3: Verify

Re-check CI status using the commands from Section 4 above.

### Auto-Fix Loop Pattern

When asked to auto-fix CI, follow this loop:

1. Check CI status → identify failures
2. Read failure logs → understand the error
3. Use `read_file` + `patch`/`write_file` → fix the code
4. `git add . && git commit -m "fix: ..." && git push`
5. Wait for CI → re-check status
6. Repeat if still failing (up to 3 attempts, then ask the user)

## 6. Merging

**With gh:**

```bash
# Squash merge + delete branch (cleanest for feature branches)
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch

# Enable auto-merge (merges when all checks pass)
gh pr merge --auto --squash --delete-branch
```

**With git + curl:**

```bash
PR_NUMBER=<number>

# Merge the PR via API (squash)
curl -s -X PUT \
  -H "Authorization: token $GITHUB_TOKEN" \
  https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/pulls/$PR_NUMBER/merge \
  -d "{
    \"merge_method\": \"squash\",
```

{"content": "1|---
2|name: skill-pre-deploy-verification
3|description: Mandatory verification checklist before pushing to a deploy-tracked repo; prevents the most common first-deploy failures.
4|source: canon
5|canon_version: HEAD
6|---
7|
8|# Skill: Pre-Deploy Verification
9|
10|Mandatory verification checklist before pushing code to a deploy-tracked repo. Prevents the most common first-deploy failures observed across sessions.
11|
12|---
13|
14|## When to Use
15|
16|**Before every `git push` to a branch that will trigger CI/CD on a deploy-tracked repo.** No exceptions. Run through this checklist after all code changes are complete and before creating the PR.
17|
18|This skill complements the DONE gate in `skill-change-tracking.md`, that gate verifies *after* deploy; this skill prevents deploy failures *before* they happen.
19|
20|**Position in the 6-stage flow (`principles-base.md §12`):** this skill is the stage-4 precondition, it runs between stage 2 (local validation) and stage 4 (PR open → CI green → user merge click). Deploy itself is always user-triggered (a merge click or explicit deploy action), never arm auto-merge, never push directly to a protected branch. The post-merge re-validation at stage 5 is a separate check on trunk; this skill does not replace it.
21|
22|---
23|
24|## Prerequisites
25|
26|Before running this checklist, the engineer MUST have read `infra.md` (or the project's equivalent infrastructure playbook) for the current session. Many pre-deploy failures are caused by not knowing the deploy pipeline mechanics. If you haven't read it → read it now before proceeding.
27|
28|---
29|
30|## Instructions
31|
32|### 1. Lint Check (Local)
33|
34|Run the project's linter locally before pushing. Do not rely on CI to catch lint errors.
35|
36|```/dev/null/lint-check.sh#L1-2
37|# Python services (42Bros pattern)
38|ruff check .
39|```
40|
41|Common failures: line length, unused imports, import ordering, missing blank lines between import groups.
42|
43|### 2. Import Path Verification
44|
45|Verify all import paths will resolve correctly **inside Docker**, not just locally.
46|
47|- [ ] If the service has `src/__init__.py` (package mode) → all internal imports MUST be **relative** (`from .settings import settings`, not `from settings import settings`)
48|- [ ] If the service does NOT have `src/__init__.py` → absolute imports are correct (`from settings import settings`)
49|- [ ] No imports reference local filesystem paths or dev-only modules
50|
51|**Why this fails:** Local Python resolves imports differently than Docker's `WORKDIR` + `CMD` combination. Absolute imports work locally but crash in Docker when `src/` is a package.
52|
53|### 3. Dependency Verification
54|
55|- [ ] Every `import` statement in the codebase has a corresponding dependency in `pyproject.toml` (or is a stdlib module)
56|- [ ] If a new dependency was added → `poetry lock` has been run and `poetry.lock` is committed
57|- [ ] If using `b42_common` → the git tag pin in `pyproject.toml` matches the version that contains the features you're using
58|
59|**Why this fails:** Code works locally because the package exists in the dev venv, but the Docker build only installs what `pyproject.toml` declares.
60|
61|### 4. Environment Variable & Secrets Verification
62|
63|- [ ] Every env var the code reads at startup (via `BaseSettings`, `os.getenv`, or config loaders) is present in **one** of:
64|  - The deploy workflow's `.env` generation step (fetched from Vault or GH secrets)
65|  - The `docker-compose.prod.yml` environment section
66|  - A config file that is SCP'd or volume-mounted
67|- [ ] If a new Vault secret was added → the Vault path exists and the deploy workflow reads from the correct path
68|- [ ] If a new GitHub Actions secret was added → it exists in the repo's settings and is referenced in `deploy.yml`
69|
70|**Why this fails:** Deploy workflows write `.env` from scratch using only the secrets they know about. A new env var in code without a corresponding deploy workflow update = crash-loop on deploy.
71|
72|### 5. Payload & Contract Verification
73|
74|When the change involves inter-service communication (RabbitMQ messages, REST API calls, Valkey keys):
75|
76|- [ ] Publisher payload schema matches what consumers expect (field names, types, nesting structure)
77|- [ ] If a field was renamed → all consumers handle both old and new names (dual-key pattern) OR all consumers are deployed first
78|- [ ] If a new RabbitMQ exchange/queue was added → the exchange exists on the broker (created by the publishing service or IaC)
79|
80|**Why this fails:** Publisher sends `{funding_rate: 0.01}` flat; consumer expects `{BTC: {funding_rate: 0.01}}` nested. Works in unit tests with mocked data, fails in production.
81|
82|### 6. Deploy Workflow Verification
83|
84|- [ ] `deploy.yml` references the correct Vault secret path for this service
85|- [ ] Docker image name in `deploy.yml` matches `docker-compose.prod.yml`
86|- [ ] If the service uses Alembic → the deploy script runs migrations before starting the container (or the entrypoint handles it)
87|- [ ] `docker-compose.prod.yml` has memory limits set
88|
89|### 7. UI Validation
90|
91|**Mandatory whenever the change affects a rendered page, overlay, route transition, redirect, toast, loading state, form submission, or any visible or behavioral surface.** N/A only for purely invisible backend changes, internal refactors, server-only log changes, schema/migration with no UI effect.
92|
93|- [ ] Browser MCP validation run against the change, flow exercised end-to-end on the actual dev server, not just unit tests
94|- [ ] Evidence captured to the project's artifact directory per `../reference/guidelines-browser-testing.md §4`, screenshots, console dump, network list; perf trace if performance is in scope
95|- [ ] Evidence paths linked from the block's Completion Report (path-only in chat per `principles-base.md §12`)
96|- [ ] Decision-framework respected, devtools-class MCP for perf/throttling/heap/Lighthouse/attach-to-session; automation-class MCP for scripted multi-step flows
97|- [ ] **MCP-failure rule.** If the contracted verification method (per the block's Acceptance Criteria) cannot be executed because the MCP is unavailable: STOP. Do not silently substitute the other MCP, do not proceed with "code-review-instead." Escalate to user with: contracted method · failure reason · proposed alternative · cost/time impact. User decides whether to renegotiate the AC, defer the block, or troubleshoot the MCP. This is the §11 "no silent scope downgrade" rule applied at the pre-deploy gate.
98|
99|See `../reference/guidelines-browser-testing.md` for capability matrix, decision framework, and setup.
100|
101|---
102|
103|## Constraints
104|
105|- This checklist is a **gate**, not a suggestion. Do not push until all applicable items pass.
106|- Items that don't apply to the current change can be skipped (e.g., skip §5 if no inter-service communication changed).
107|- Do NOT run `ruff check` on repos you didn't change, only on the repo being pushed.
108|- This skill does NOT replace the DONE gate (`skill-change-tracking.md` §Final). This runs *before* push; the DONE gate runs *after* deploy.
109|- **Post-merge re-validation (stage 5 of the 6-stage flow)**, after the user clicks Merge, re-run acceptance criteria (and browser MCPs for UI) on trunk. A regression opens a new feature branch and re-enters the flow from stage 1; Done is not marked while a regression is open. This re-validation is owned by the project's session-end skill (§0 in the engineer session-end template), not by this pre-deploy skill, but it is the check that actually gates stage 5.
110|
111|---
112|
113|## Error Handling
114|
115|- **Lint fails:** Fix all errors before pushing. Do not push with `# noqa` unless the suppression is justified and documented.
116|- **Import path uncertain:** Check the Dockerfile's `WORKDIR` and the presence of `__init__.py` in the source directory. When in doubt, match the pattern used by existing services in the same project.
117|- **Missing env var in deploy workflow:** Add it to `deploy.yml` now, do not defer. If the value comes from Vault, verify the Vault path exists. If the value is a new GH secret, add it to the repo before pushing.
118|- **Payload schema mismatch:** If the change is a rename, implement the dual-key backward-compatible pattern (consumers accept both old and new names). Deploy consumers before publisher.
119|
120|---
121|
122|**Last Updated:** 2026-05-05, §7 MCP-failure rule tightened: STOP + escalate when contracted method cannot run (no silent substitution). 2026-04-23, added §7 UI Validation (mandatory browser MCP validation for any UI-touching or visible-behavior change). 2026-04-23, aligned to 6-stage flow: When to Use now cites stage-4 position; §Constraints names stage 5 post-merge re-validation as the downstream gate.", "total_lines": 122, "file_size": 8577, "truncated": false, "is_binary": false, "is_image": false, "not_found": false}
